extracted.intended_audience: student journalists / reporters learning crime and police reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples for writing police/crime news stories (arrests, forgery, embezzlement, burglary, hold-ups) with emphasis on follow-ups, human detail, evidence and chronology. Uses illustrative published items to show good practice on the police beat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write prompt follow-up stories when new information arrives
rubrics_metrics.description: Note — How, with additional information, a striking follow-up story can be written a few hours after the first story was published is well illustrated by the following two stories, the first of which appeared in the Saturday evening edition and the second in the Sunday morning edition of the same paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When more facts become available (arrests, discovered evidence, confessions), publish a follow-up quickly that adds the new information and reshapes the narrative; use new editions or later editions to update readers and deepen the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with the immediate newsworthy action (arrest/incident) and follow with background
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories open with the arrest or the crime (e.g., "She was arrested this morning...", "John E. Jones, jr. ... is being detained this afternoon pending an investigation").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with the most immediate facts (who, what, where, when) then supply context and background (motive, past record, circumstances) to explain how the event came about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include concrete identifying details (names, ages, addresses, affiliations)
rubrics_metrics.description: News items repeatedly give full identifying details: names, ages, addresses, employers or company affiliations (e.g., "Laura Walsington, 20 years old, 14 West Thirty-second Street", "Henry A. Black, 47, smart lawyer").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific identifiers to make the report verifiable and informative to readers; attribute positions (bank clerk, lawyer) and social ties (wife, pastor) where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify losses and values precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports enumerate amounts and values (e.g., forged checks from $15 to $75; checks aggregating $119; discrepancy amounting to something like $9,000; diamonds and other stones to the value of $3500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give precise monetary figures, counts and valuations of stolen or embezzled property to convey the scale of the crime and its impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe the method, means and physical evidence of the crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories describe how crimes were committed and what physical evidence exists (e.g., forgery method of practicing signatures and telephoning the bank; burglar used a key and screwdriver; "excellent set of finger prints on a hand mirror").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain modus operandi, tools used, hiding places, and any forensic clues (fingerprints, mask, weapon) to give readers a clear picture of the criminal act and the investigatory leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report investigative and policing steps (detention, interrogation, evidence custody)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts detail police actions and procedures: arrests, being taken to police headquarters, detention pending investigation, detectives questioning, checks found in safes, evidence examined (e.g., finger prints found by Detective M. T. Arey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include procedural milestones (when and where suspects were detained, who questioned them, what evidence was recovered and by whom) to show how the case is developing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotes and confessions to humanize and explain motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters include suspects' or victims' words and pleas (e.g., "'I'll pay it all back,' she cried... 'Only give me another chance.'", "'I was going to be married and knew I would need a lot of money,' said Russell.").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include representative quotations that reveal motive, remorse, denial or explanation — they add voice and credibility but should be clearly attributed and placed in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include human-interest scene detail and emotional reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Pieces emphasize scenes and feelings: "Slumped down in a chair... she wept bitterly." "In the matron’s room at the jail were the boy and his wife. They had been crying." "Two pairs of arms entwined the neck of Harry Blair..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory, emotional and domestic detail to make crime stories resonate with readers, but balance color with factual accuracy and avoid gratuitous sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use eyewitness accounts and identifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories rely on witness identification and immediate eyewitness testimony (e.g., the little girl who found the burglar; Mathis identifying a robber; victims shouting and calling police).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite eyewitnesses and their identifications clearly, noting circumstances of identification and any uncertainties to avoid misreporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative/scene structure can be used to dramatize complex incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Some accounts use a dramatic, multi-scene structure to tell the story (e.g., the Kansas City "See now how real life beats the reel life" series with REAL I–IV scenes showing sequence and irony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For feature-style or longer crime pieces, organize material into scenes and episodes to build narrative tension while preserving factual chronology and attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report outcomes and legal process steps (charges, confinement, arraignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles note legal consequences: suspects being held, jailed overnight, to be charged with a felony, confined until arraignment, committed for ten days, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow through to report official outcomes (charges filed, arraignments, confinement) so readers understand the legal status and next steps in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context that explains motive or social causes (poverty, liquor, desperation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports often contextualize criminal acts with social causes cited by suspects or others (e.g., 'Sister sick. No work. Money gone.'; many suspects blame liquor or lack of work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include accountable context (economic pressure, addiction) when relevant to the story, but distinguish between defendants' explanations and corroborated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document how suspects were captured (leads, descriptions, pursuit, accidental recovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories explain capture mechanics: descriptions relayed by telephone to patrols, suspects run into fences, an auto runs over a victim, policeman shoots and a mask is found, routine patrols observe suspicious persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the chain of events and police tactics that led to apprehension — e.g., circulation of descriptions, witness cooperation, patrol work — to show investigative work behind the arrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute reports to originating publications and editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many pieces are prefaced by source lines: 'Kansas City Star', 'Topeka Capital', 'San Francisco Chronicle', and sometimes by edition (e.g., 'Saturday evening edition', 'Sunday morning edition').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reprinting or summarizing, attribute material to the original newspaper/edition; this maintains transparency about sourcing and edition-specific updates.
